text: You already know this pattern cold: a CASE expression with two branches, picking one label or another based on a single condition. Products over a thousand dollars get called Premium, everything else gets called Standard.

IIF does the exact same job, just shorter. Condition first, then the value to use if it's true, then the value to use otherwise. If the condition is false, or even NULL or unknown, you get the false branch -- exactly how CASE's WHEN already behaves. It's a direct, drop-in shorthand, nothing more.

You can nest IIF calls inside each other to handle three or more branches, and it works -- but readability drops fast once you do. The equivalent CASE expression with multiple WHEN clauses stays clear no matter how many branches you add, which is usually the better call past two options.

IIF arrived in SQL Server 2012 as shorthand for exactly this two-branch pattern, familiar from tools like Excel and Access. It's pure syntax sugar -- SQL Server compiles it down to the same CASE expression internally, so there's no performance difference, only a readability tradeoff in each direction. Next up, CHOOSE -- a different kind of shorthand for picking a value out of a list by its position.
